title: Interactive Cross-modal Learning for Text-3D Scene Retrieval

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text introduces a reference '[60] Zhang, L., Wang, M., & Liu, Q. (2022). Bayesian Density Correction for Cross-Modal Retrieval. In Proceedings of ICLR 2022.' inline in the body text, in addition to citing it as [44, 60]. This reference does not appear in the paper's actual reference list (which ends at [59]), and the in-text format (giving a full bibliographic citation mid-paragraph rather than in the references section) is inconsistent with the rest of the paper, strongly suggesting a fabricated/invented citation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.2.1, Density Compensated Factor and corrected similarity formula
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper defines ρ(v_i) = 1/((1/k)Σ D(v_i,v_j)+ε), which is LARGE when average neighbor distance is SMALL (i.e., in high-density regions). The corrected similarity is S̃ = S·sqrt(ρ(v_j)), meaning high-density regions get a LARGER multiplicative factor and thus an INCREASED similarity score. However, the text claims 'This formulation ensures that high-density regions receive appropriately reduced similarity scores, consistent with our bias mitigation objective,' which directly contradicts the mathematical behavior of the formula.

The minimum enclosing hypersphere constraint is written as 'u_i^j o_i^\top ≤ R_i, ∀j', using an inner product between the feature and center compared directly to a radius. A valid enclosing-hypersphere constraint (as in SVDD, ref [46]) should use a squared distance/norm, e.g., ||u_i^j - o_i||^2 ≤ R_i^2. As written, the inner-product-based constraint does not correctly express hypersphere containment and is mathematically inconsistent with the cited SVDD formulation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2 (RoMa baseline row) vs Table 1 (RoMa row)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 1 reports RoMa's coarse-grained results as ScanRefer R@1/R@5/R@10/Rsum = 11.4/34.8/54.4/100.6 and Nr3D = 6.5/24.8/37.6/68.9. In Table 2, the RoMa baseline row instead lists ScanRefer values 9.7/33.1/50.2/93.0 (identical to the VSE∞ row directly above it) and Nr3D values 8.3/27.9/37.2/73.4, neither of which matches Table 1's RoMa numbers. This is an internal contradiction between two tables reporting the same baseline method on the same datasets.

The abstract claims IDeal 'completely solves the alignment challenge between texts and 3D scenes through continuous interaction, achieving near-perfect retrieval accuracy across diverse query types.' However, the best reported results (Table 1) show R@1 of only 37.8% (ScanRefer, fine-grained) and much lower for coarse-grained settings (12.8% R@1), far from 'near-perfect.' This claim is also contradicted by the paper's own Limitations section stating 'the performance of the methods is relatively low.'

The paper claims the Hierarchical Scene Reconstruction strategy 'represent[s] a significant advancement over standard CoT approaches,' yet the ablation in Table 3 shows removing CoT ('w/o CoT') only reduces Rsum from 196.0 to 193.1, a modest ~1.5% difference, which does not support characterizing the improvement as a 'significant advancement.'

The text states 'the LLMs tend to focus on the salient objects in the scene and ignore the fine-grained details from a scene-level perspective, limiting the depth and breadth of LLM interaction, as demonstrated in Table 1.' Table 1 is a quantitative results table (R@1/R@5/R@10/Rsum comparisons) and does not demonstrate this qualitative behavior; the actual illustrative evidence (e.g., MERLIN generating redundant local descriptions) appears in Figure 5, not Table 1.

L_dis = -Σ y_ij log S(ũ_i, v_j) takes the logarithm directly of a similarity score S, which (as cosine similarity or raw dot-product similarity as used elsewhere, e.g., Eq. 2/3 exponentiate S before normalizing) can be negative or zero, making log(S) undefined or complex-valued; no normalization (e.g., softmax) is applied before the log as it is in Eq. (3), creating a mathematical inconsistency in how S is used across the paper.

The paper states 'Ethical approval for this study was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of Sichuan University (Protocol #SCU-2024-IRB-089). No new human subjects data was collected.' This is self-contradictory/suspicious: IRB approval is typically required only when human-subjects data is collected or human participants are involved, yet the paper only uses pre-existing public 3D scene/text datasets (ScanNet, ScanRefer, Nr3D, Sr3D) and explicitly states no new human data was collected, making the cited specific IRB protocol irrelevant or fabricated.
